ch16.anchor: a pair of mandarin ducks sharing one fate
ch16.note: Mandarin ducks, believed to pair for life, are the Chinese emblem of a devoted married couple; 'a pair of mandarin ducks sharing one fate' means husband and wife going to their deaths together—here Wang Jingwei and Chen Bijun.

ch16.anchor: the Canton rising of the twenty-ninth of the third month
ch16.note: The Huanghuagang ('Yellow Flower Mound') Uprising of the 29th day of the third lunar month, 27 April 1911: a doomed Tongmenghui revolt at Guangzhou whose fallen were enshrined as the 'seventy-two martyrs,' among the most revered sacrifices of the republican revolution. It is distinct from the Communists' 1927 Guangzhou Uprising.
The old Chinese day was divided into twelve two-hour periods named for the zodiac animals. The hour of the ox is about 1–3 a.m.; the hour of the monkey, named later, about 3–5 p.m.
The Yellow Emperor (黄帝, Huangdi) is the legendary common ancestor of the Chinese people; 'sons of the Yellow Emperor' is a rhetorical way of saying the Chinese as a nation.

The Nanhua Ribao (南华日报, 'South China Daily'), a Hong Kong newspaper founded in 1930 by Wang Jingwei's close associate Lin Bosheng and made the mouthpiece of Wang's pro-Japanese 'peace movement'; it was where his notorious peace telegram first appeared in December 1938.

Wen Shengcai (温生才, 1870–1911), a returned overseas laborer who in April 1911 shot dead the Manchu general Fu Qi at Guangzhou and was executed for it, honored thereafter among the martyrs of the revolution—cited here as a model of the patriot-assassin.

Yi Wan-yong (이완용 / 李完用, 1858–1926), the Korean prime minister who signed the 1910 treaty surrendering Korea to Japanese annexation—throughout East Asia the byword for a statesman who hands his own country to a foreign power.

Puyi (溥仪, 1906–1967), the last emperor of the Qing, deposed as a child in the 1911 Revolution and installed by Japan in 1932 as the figurehead 'emperor' of Manchukuo—cited here as the type of the puppet ruler.

Wu Sangui (吴三桂, 1612–1678), the Ming general who in 1644 opened the Shanhai Pass and let the Manchu armies through to conquer China. His name is the standard label for one who invites a foreign force in to overthrow his own dynasty.

Sun Wukong, the Monkey King of the novel Journey to the West, master of seventy-two transformations who could never, however, hide his monkey's tail—hence the jibe that Wang, shift his shape as he might, cannot conceal what he really is.
